exam: What are the key steps in managing a large facial furuncle? — I&D, avoid squeezing, start systemic antibiotics covering MRSA, monitor for cavernous sinus thrombosis.
How would you differentiate a furuncle from folliculitis on examination? — Furuncle has a fluctuant centre and deeper tenderness; folliculitis is superficial with papules and no pus cavity.

A diabetic patient presents with a 3 cm painful nodule on the thigh and fever. Which investigations are essential? — CBC, pus culture, blood glucose, HIV test if risk; results guide antibiotics and glycaemic control.

Why is incision and drainage preferred over oral antibiotics alone for a carbuncle? — Drainage removes pus, reduces bacterial load, and speeds healing; antibiotics alone cannot penetrate an established abscess.
What complications should you watch for after I&D of a furuncle in the facial danger triangle? — Cavernous sinus thrombosis, orbital cellulitis, spread to deep facial veins.
Explain why clindamycin may be chosen in a community with high MRSA prevalence. — It covers MRSA and also suppresses toxin production, useful for PVL‑positive strains.

A patient reports recurrent boils despite good hygiene. What long‑term measures reduce recurrence? — Nasal mupirocin decolonisation, treat underlying diabetes, weight control, avoid shared personal items.

In a low‑resource setting without culture facilities, how would you decide on empiric therapy? — Use local antibiogram data; if MRSA rates >20 % choose clindamycin or TMP‑SMX, otherwise use a beta‑lactam active against MSSA.
ai.title: Furuncle (Boil)
ai.subject: Surgery
ai.summary: A furuncle is a deep skin abscess centred on a hair follicle, most often caused by Staphylococcus aureus. It presents as a painful, erythematous nodule that becomes fluctuant and drains pus.

b: Fluctuance on palpation indicates a pus cavity
Central yellow head suggests drainage point
sections.p: A furuncle is a localized collection of pus within the dermis and subcutaneous tissue that originates from an infected hair follicle. Diagnosis is clinical: a tender, erythematous nodule that becomes fluctuant with a central pus point.

b: Simple: local pain, no fever
Large: fever, lymphangitis, >2 cm
Carbuncle: multiple nodes, systemic toxicity
sections.p: Severity is graded by size, depth, and presence of systemic signs. Simple furuncle: <2 cm, no systemic features. Large furuncle: 2–5 cm, may have regional lymphadenopathy. Carbuncle: multiple coalescing furuncles, >5 cm, often with fever.

b: S. aureus – skin coloniser, most frequent
Streptococcus pyogenes – especially in children
Gram‑negative rods – in HIV, chronic ulcers
sections.p: The predominant pathogen is Staphylococcus aureus, including MRSA and PVL‑positive strains. Streptococci and Gram‑negative bacilli are less common but important in immunocompromised patients.

b: Painful, warm, erythematous nodule
Fluctuant centre with yellow pus
Regional lymphadenopathy if large
sections.p: Patients report a tender, red bump that enlarges over 2–3 days, becomes firm, then fluctuant with a central pustule that may spontaneously rupture. Common sites are neck, face, axilla, buttock, and thigh.

b: Pus culture is gold standard when available
CBC helps decide need for systemic antibiotics
sections.p: If laboratory facilities are unavailable, treat empirically based on typical flora and local resistance patterns.

t.a: Gram stain and culture of pus
t.b: Identify causative organism and antibiotic susceptibility; guides targeted therapy
Screen for diabetes, a predisposing factor
Detect immunosuppression that may alter organism profile

b: Rapid spread to facial “danger triangle” → cavernous sinus thrombosis
Extensive cellulitis or necrotizing fasciitis
Sepsis: fever, tachycardia, hypotension
sections.p: Complications arise from spread to deeper structures or systemic seeding.

b: Incision and drainage (I&D) under aseptic technique; primary goal is pus evacuation
Empiric oral antibiotics: cloxacillin or dicloxacillin for MSSA; trimethoprim‑sulfamethoxazole or clindamycin if MRSA prevalence is high
Avoid topical antiseptics that delay drainage
Control diabetes, improve nutrition, advise hygiene, decolonise nasal carriage with mupirocin if recurrent
sections.p: Treat the infection, relieve the abscess, and address predisposing factors.

Educate on hand washing, personal towels, and wound care

sections.p: Re‑examine 48–72 h after I&D to ensure healing and no new lesions.

Carbuncle – cluster of furuncles, larger, systemic signs

sections.p: Differential diagnoses share a pustular appearance but differ in depth or etiology.
